newsitem.title: USA: U.S. officials say Japan car trade pact successful.
newsitem.headline: U.S. officials say Japan car trade pact successful.

text.p: U.S. officials said Tuesday the U.S. car industry, which was on its back just a decade ago, is now doing "phenomenally" well and that a year-old car trade pact with Japan has been a success.

In an upbeat election-year assessment of an industry that is important to the Midwest industrial states that President Clinton wants to win in November, a U.S. Commerce Department report said the United States is producing more vehicles than Japan for the first time since 1979.

"The auto industry is in phenomenal shape," U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor told a news conference. "It is reporting record profits, strong sales, rapidly expanding exports and robust employment. Employment is at a 17-year high in the auto industry."
Kantor and other U.S. trade officials said a 1995 trade agreement with Tokyo has helped open Japan's market to more U.S.-made vehicles and parts and that they expect the gains to continue.

"By virtually all measures the agreement has been a success," said one senior U.S. trade official. "Significant gains have been made in opening Japan's auto markets, and we will continue to see those gains over the course of the auto agreement."

U.S. and Japanese trade officials are to meet Wednesday and Thursday in San Francisco to review the year-old accord that was reached just as Washington was about to impose punitive tariffs on Japanese luxury car imports.
Joining in on the discussions will be representatives from from Canada, Australia and the European Union, even though Europeans sharply criticized U.S. tactics in the showdown with Japan over cars.

Trade has not been a major issue so far this election year, but Republican candidate Bob Dole has been critical of Clinton's record and has vowed to make a case in upcoming debates for a more aggressive trade policy.

U.S. trade officials said last year's agreement with Japan has been successful in opening the second-largest car market in the world to more foreign competitors. They said automotive imports from Japan are down, while North American exports to Japan are up.

Little more than a decade ago the U.S. industry lost much its market to more-competitive Japanese manufacturers and Chrysler Corp. C.N and Ford Motor Co. F.N went through wrenching restructurings that included major layoffs.

Kantor told reporters that the stronger dollar has not hurt U.S. car sales to Japan even though U.S. manufacturers have voiced strong concern that the currency's rising value will make their products too costly and undermine recent gains.

Last year some 142,000 cars were shipped from North America to Japan. Of that, 58,000 were made by General Motors Corp., GM.N Ford and Chrysler, while the rest were shipped by Japanese manufacturers with North American plants, officials said.

So far this year, Big Three exports from North America are up 40 percent, with some 37,000 cars shipped to Japan in the first seven months. Japanese manufacturers exported 40,000 cars in that period, they said.
U.S. manufacturers have also expressed concern about the number of new Japanese dealerships selling their vehicles.

The United States set a goal of 200 new dealerships by the end of this year. So far little more than half of that number has been achieved and car and the American Automobile Manufacturers Association complained that they are having little success signing up dealers associated with Toyota and other Japanese manufacturers.
"We would be concerned if that (the dealership goal) was not met by the end of the year," Kantor said. "We would like to see continued progress."
